```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Before harnessr sends a request, it looks the model up in its registry. The
entry gives the model's context window and output cap, which size every prompt,
and the prices you set, which turn the tokens a request used into dollars and
let `max_cost_usd` hold. The tokens come from a token counter, the same one
that measures a prompt before it goes out.

This guide covers all three: what the registry knows about a model and how
sure it is, how to add a model and set the prices you pay, what a cost estimate
says and when it is `NA`, and how harnessr counts tokens. Every example runs
offline with no API key. The prices in it are illustrative: use your provider's
current prices, in US dollars per million tokens.

## Setting up

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE)
```

`hr_options()` returns the values it replaced, and the last chunk of this guide
puts them back with `hr_options(old)`. Every registration below lasts for the
R session and changes nothing on disk.

## What harnessr knows about a model

`hr_models()` lists the registry, one row per model, chat models first:

```{r}
m <- hr_models()
nrow(m)
table(m$kind)
m[m$id %in% c("gpt-5.6-terra", "gpt-4o", "gpt-4", "text-embedding-3-small"), ]
```

harnessr ships `r nrow(m)` models, `r sum(m$kind == "chat")` chat models and
`r sum(m$kind == "embedding")` embedding models, all OpenAI's, read from `inst/extdata/models.csv` when the package loads. For each
it ships the limits: `context_window` (prompt and reply together, in tokens),
`max_output` (the most tokens one reply may have), whether it is a reasoning
model and, for an embedding model, its dimensions. The price columns are `NA`
because harnessr ships no prices. The table leaves out
`supports_temperature` and `dimensions`; `hr_model_info()` has every field. For a model with no price, `as_of` is the
month its limits were last checked; once you set prices, it is the month of
the prices.

gpt-4 lists an output cap equal to its window. A prompt to it still has room:
`hr_budget()` reserves a quarter of the usable window for the reply, not the
whole cap:

```{r}
unlist(hr_budget("gpt-4")[c("context_window", "input", "output")])
```

A tenth of the window is left unused, for error in the token count (see
[Counting tokens](#counting-tokens)).

### One model: `hr_model_info()`

`hr_model_info()` returns one model's entry as a list:

```{r}
str(hr_model_info("gpt-5.6-terra"))
```

Three fields here change how a request is built. A model with `reasoning =
TRUE` gets no `temperature`, and its output cap is raised to at least the
`reasoning_floor` option (2,048 tokens) where the window has room, because its
reasoning is billed as output inside the same cap. A model with
`supports_temperature = FALSE` gets no `temperature` either. `kind` says
whether the model answers prompts or returns embeddings.

`source` says where the entry came from, and `certain` says whether harnessr
knows the model or guessed. harnessr tries five places in order and stops at
the first that has the id:

| `source` | where the entry came from | `certain` |
|---|---|---|
| `"registered"` | `hr_register_model()` or `hr_load_models()` in this session | `TRUE` |
| `"builtin"` | the shipped file | `TRUE` |
| `"alias"` | a dated or alternative name for a model above, such as `"chatgpt-4o-latest"` for gpt-4o | `TRUE` |
| `"pattern:..."` | a family pattern that matches the id, such as `^gpt-4o` | `FALSE` |
| `"default"` | nothing matched: a 128,000-token window and a 4,096-token output cap | `FALSE` |

A registered entry wins over a built-in one. An alias takes its target's
entry, a registered one first, and keeps its own name as `id`:

```{r}
str(hr_model_info("chatgpt-4o-latest")[c("id", "context_window", "max_output",
                                         "source", "certain")])
```

An id the registry does not hold gets a guess, with a warning of class
`gr_unknown_model`. A dated gpt-4o name the registry has not heard of matches
the `^gpt-4o` pattern:

```{r}
str(hr_model_info("gpt-4o-2027-01-15")[c("context_window", "max_output",
                                         "source", "certain")])
```

An id that matches no pattern gets the default profile:

```{r}
str(hr_model_info("acme-chat-7")[c("context_window", "max_output", "source",
                                   "certain")])
```

The warning repeats on every call that names the model, so a run that uses an
unknown id says so for each request. Read it as "check this before you trust a
budget or a cost": a guessed window can be far from the real one, and a
guessed entry has no price. A typo shows up the same way, and its guess can look
right. `"gpt-5.6-tera"` matches the `^gpt-5\.6` family and gets
gpt-5.6-terra's window, but no price you set for gpt-5.6-terra reaches it.

To stop instead of guessing, set `unknown_model_action` to `"error"`. A lookup
of an unknown id then raises an error of class `gr_unknown_model`, and so does
`hr_call()` before it sends anything:

```{r}
prev <- hr_options(unknown_model_action = "error")
tryCatch(hr_model_info("gpt-5.6-tera"),
         gr_unknown_model = function(e) class(e))
hr_options(prev)
```

### Two limits: `hr_model_limits()`

`hr_model_limits()` returns the window and the output cap alone:

```{r}
hr_model_limits("gpt-4o")
```

The second element is named `output_tokens`, not `max_output` as in
`hr_model_info()`. It goes through the same lookup, so an unknown id warns
here too.

## Adding a model or changing one

`hr_register_model()` adds an entry or changes one. It does not check the
figures with the provider: what you give is what harnessr uses.

### A model harnessr does not know

A model behind a company gateway, or a local one, needs both limits.
`reasoning`, `supports_temperature`, `kind` and `dimensions` default to a chat
model that takes a temperature:

```{r}
hr_register_model("gateway-chat", context_window = 200000, max_output = 8192)
str(hr_model_info("gateway-chat")[c("context_window", "max_output", "reasoning",
                                    "supports_temperature", "source", "certain")])
```

A reasoning model behind the gateway says so, and an embedding model gives its
kind and dimensions:

```{r}
hr_register_model("gateway-reasoner", context_window = 128000, max_output = 16000,
                  reasoning = TRUE, supports_temperature = FALSE)
hr_register_model("gateway-embed", context_window = 8192, max_output = 0,
                  kind = "embedding", dimensions = 1024)
```

harnessr refuses a chat model whose output cap is as large as its window,
because then no room would be left for a prompt:

```{r}
tryCatch(hr_register_model("too-small", context_window = 4096, max_output = 4096),
         error = conditionMessage)
```

### A change to one field of a known model

Leave out either limit, and `hr_register_model()` changes the current entry,
built in or registered, keeping every value you leave out. To hold gpt-4o's
replies to 8,000 tokens:

```{r}
hr_register_model("gpt-4o", max_output = 8000)
str(hr_model_info("gpt-4o")[c("context_window", "max_output", "source")])
```

The entry is now registered, and it wins over the built-in one until the
session ends. A model with no entry to change is an error that says what to
give:

```{r}
tryCatch(hr_register_model("never-seen", max_output = 8000), error = conditionMessage)
```

An alias has no entry of its own, so a change to it is refused with its target
named:

```{r}
tryCatch(hr_register_model("chatgpt-4o-latest", input_usd = 2.5, output_usd = 10),
         error = conditionMessage)
```

## Prices

### Why harnessr ships none

Providers change prices more often than harnessr is released. A price list in
the package would be wrong for most of its life, and a wrong price moves the
point where `max_cost_usd` stops a run. A missing price shows: the cost comes
out `NA`. A wrong one gives a figure that looks right. So harnessr ships
limits, which change rarely, and you set the prices you pay.

### Setting one model's prices

`input_usd` and `output_usd` are US dollars per million tokens. For a known
model, the prices are all you give:

```{r}
# Illustrative figures: use your provider's current prices.
hr_register_model("gpt-4o-mini", input_usd = 0.15, output_usd = 0.60)
str(hr_model_info("gpt-4o-mini")[c("context_window", "max_output", "input_usd",
                                   "output_usd", "as_of", "source")])
```

The model keeps its limits, and the entry is stamped with the current month.
Four rules hold for every price:

- A chat model needs both prices, or neither. Half a price is an error,
  because a cost with half its price missing cannot be estimated. An
  embedding model needs only `input_usd`, since it returns no output tokens.
- `cached_input_usd` sets a rate for input the provider served from its prompt
  cache. Without it, cached input is priced as other input, which never
  undercounts.
- A local model costs nothing: give it `input_usd = 0` and `output_usd = 0`.
  Its cost is then 0, not `NA`, and the spending limit counts it at zero with
  no warning.
- When you change a priced entry, a price you leave out keeps its value. If
  the change sets only some of the prices, the entry keeps the older month,
  because the prices you left out are as old as before.

```{r}
tryCatch(hr_register_model("gpt-4.1-mini", input_usd = 0.40), error = conditionMessage)
hr_register_model("local-llama", context_window = 32768, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 0, output_usd = 0)
# Illustrative figure.
hr_register_model("gateway-embed", input_usd = 0.05)
```

### Setting many prices from a file: `hr_load_models()`

`hr_load_models()` reads a CSV file with a header row and registers each row as
`hr_register_model()` would. `id` is the only column every file needs, and a
blank cell, or `NA`, means the value is not given:

| column | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `id` | the model id, exactly as the API expects it; each id once |
| `input_usd`, `output_usd` | price per million tokens, in USD; both for a chat model, or neither |
| `cached_input_usd` | price per million input tokens served from the provider's prompt cache |
| `as_of` | the month you checked the prices, as `YYYY-MM`; blank stamps the current month, and a later month is an error |
| `context_window`, `max_output` | limits in tokens; both for a model harnessr does not know |
| `reasoning`, `supports_temperature` | `TRUE` or `FALSE` |
| `kind` | `chat` or `embedding` |
| `dimensions` | how many dimensions an embedding model's vectors have |

A row that leaves a limit blank changes the model's current entry, as
`hr_register_model()` does without one. A row that gives both limits registers
the model in full. This file prices two built-in chat models, with a cached
input rate for one, and adds a gateway model with its limits:

```{r}
prices <- file.path(tempdir(), "models-guide-prices.csv")
# Illustrative figures: use your provider's current prices.
writeLines(c(
  "id,input_usd,output_usd,cached_input_usd,context_window,max_output,as_of",
  "gpt-4o,2.50,10.00,1.25,,,",
  "gpt-5.6-terra,2,12,,,,",
  "partner-model,3,15,,200000,8192,2026-10"
), prices)
loaded <- hr_load_models(prices)
loaded
m <- hr_models()
m[m$id %in% loaded, c("id", "context_window", "max_output", "input_usd_per_1m",
                      "output_usd_per_1m", "cached_input_usd_per_1m", "as_of")]
```

`hr_load_models()` returns, invisibly, the ids it registered, in file order.
gpt-4o kept the 8,000-token output cap set earlier, because its row left the
limits blank.

harnessr checks the whole file before it registers anything. A file it cannot
use stops with an error of class `hr_bad_models_file` that names the row and
column at fault, with row 1 the first row after the header. The registry is
left as it was:

```{r}
bad <- file.path(tempdir(), "models-guide-bad.csv")
writeLines(c("id,input_usd,output_usd", "gpt-4.1,2,8", "gpt-4.1-mini,two,1.6"), bad)
err <- tryCatch(hr_load_models(bad), hr_bad_models_file = function(e) e)
conditionMessage(err)
c(row = err$row, column = err$column)
is.na(hr_model_info("gpt-4.1")$input_usd)
```

gpt-4.1, on the good first row, has no price: nothing in the file was
registered. Loading a file again replaces the entries of the models it names
and leaves the others as they are. To set the same prices in every session,
keep one file per project under version control and load it at the top of each
script, as `vignette("runs")` describes:

```{r eval = FALSE}
hr_load_models("prices.csv")
```

## What a cost estimate says: `hr_estimate_cost()`

`hr_estimate_cost()` turns token counts into dollars at the model's prices:

```{r}
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", input_tokens = 120000, output_tokens = 4000)
```

That is 120,000 input tokens at \$2.50 per million plus 4,000 output tokens at
\$10. Vectors of counts are summed, so one call prices a whole run of requests:

```{r}
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", input_tokens = c(60000, 60000), output_tokens = c(2000, 2000))
```

`cached_input_tokens` says how many of the input tokens the provider served
from its prompt cache. gpt-4o has a cached rate here, so 100,000 of the
120,000 are charged at \$1.25:

```{r}
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", 120000, 4000, cached_input_tokens = 100000)
```

A model with no cached rate charges them as other input. The estimate is `NA`,
never 0, when the model has no price, when a token count is `NA`, or when a
chat model has no output price and the call has output tokens. A local model
at zero prices costs 0:

```{r}
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4.1", 120000, 4000)
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", NA, 4000)
hr_estimate_cost("local-llama", 120000, 4000)
hr_estimate_cost("gateway-embed", 1e6)
```

`detail = TRUE` returns a data frame that also says where the figure's prices
came from: `priced` (whether the model has a price), `as_of` (the month of the
price) and `certain` (`FALSE` when the entry was guessed from a pattern or the
default):

```{r}
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", 120000, 4000, detail = TRUE)
hr_estimate_cost("acme-chat-7", 120000, 4000, detail = TRUE)
```

The second call warned that `acme-chat-7` is not in the registry, and its row
says why the figure is missing: no price, and an entry that is a guess. Every
report of a cost in dollars, such as `hr_trace_cost()`, carries the same
`priced`, `as_of` and `certain` columns. The figure is an estimate: it uses the
token counts you give and the prices you set, and it does not know about a
provider's discounts, minimum charges or taxes.

## A model with no price

A request to a chat model with no price is sent. The first request to each such
model in a session warns with class `hr_unpriced_model`, because
`max_cost_usd` cannot hold a cost it cannot compute. The mock client is exempt,
so this example uses `hr_backend_client()`, which wraps an R function as a
client that counts as paying:

```{r}
hr_register_model("unpriced-model", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096)
backend <- hr_backend_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")

tr <- hr_trace()
res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "unpriced-model", trace = tr)
res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "unpriced-model", trace = tr)
hr_trace_cost(tr)[, c("model", "calls", "paid_in", "paid_out", "usd", "priced")]
```

The two requests gave one warning. The trace counts their tokens and records their
cost as `NA`. `max_calls` and `max_tokens_total` still hold such requests, and
then `max_tokens_total` is the limit that bounds what a run spends.

`allow_unpriced = FALSE` refuses them instead. `hr_call()` then sends nothing
and returns a failed result whose `refusal` is a condition of class
`hr_unpriced_model`:

```{r}
prev <- hr_options(allow_unpriced = FALSE)
res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "unpriced-model",
               trace = hr_trace())
res$refused
class(res$refusal)
hr_options(prev)
```

`hr_governor(allow_unpriced = FALSE)` does the same for one run.
`hr_mock_client()` and replays are never refused or warned about for this, and
neither is an embedding model with no price.

## When prices go stale

The prices you set go out of date too. A cost computed from prices older than
`price_max_age_days` (120 days by default) warns with class `hr_stale_price`,
once per model per session. The age counts from the first day of the `as_of`
month. A file whose prices were checked in January 2025 shows it:

```{r}
old_prices <- file.path(tempdir(), "models-guide-old.csv")
# Illustrative figures.
writeLines(c("id,input_usd,output_usd,as_of", "gpt-4.1,2,8,2025-01"), old_prices)
hr_load_models(old_prices)
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4.1", 120000, 4000)
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4.1", 120000, 4000)
```

harnessr still returns the figure, and the second estimate does not warn
again. To clear the warning, check your provider's current prices and set them
again: `hr_register_model()` stamps the current month, and so does a row of
`hr_load_models()` with a blank `as_of`. A model with no price is never stale,
and its `as_of`, the month its limits were checked, does not count.

## Counting tokens {#counting-tokens}

harnessr counts tokens in three places: to size a prompt before it is sent,
to cut text to a number of tokens, and to fill in a usage figure the provider
did not report. All three use `hr_count_tokens()`:

```{r}
txt <- c(prose = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.",
         table = "| 2024 | 45.2 | 38.1 |",
         japanese = "東京は日本の首都です。",
         long_word = "pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis",
         blank = "")
hr_count_tokens(txt)
```

It returns one whole number per string, with blank and `NA` strings at 0.

### How exact the default count is

`hr_tokenizer()` names the counter in use:

```{r}
hr_tokenizer()
```

The default, `"heuristic"`, needs nothing installed. It does not tokenize: it
estimates, and it is built to come out high, because a count that comes out low
lets a prompt past the window and the provider rejects the request after it has
been paid for. It charges an ordinary English word at least one token, a dense
string (an id, a number, code) one token per 1.3 characters, each character
outside ASCII, such as Japanese or Cyrillic, 1.15 tokens, and an emoji 6.5. For tables, digit lists and short lines it also counts the pieces a
byte-pair tokenizer splits text into first (digit groups, punctuation runs,
line breaks) and keeps the larger figure, line by line. Each string that is not
blank then gets 3 more tokens for the framing a chat message carries.

Measured against OpenAI's `cl100k_base` and `o200k_base` encodings, it comes
in at or above the real count on tables, digit lists, tab-separated text and
short punctuated lines. Rare long words are where it
can fall short: on a table of medical terms it came in about a tenth under.
The `safety_margin` option, a tenth of the window by default, is the room
`hr_budget()` leaves for that error.

The two other built-in counters are cruder. `"words"` counts words, and
`"chars"` divides the characters by 4:

```{r}
prev_tok <- hr_tokenizer()
counts <- sapply(c("heuristic", "words", "chars"), function(t) {
  hr_set_tokenizer(t)
  hr_count_tokens(txt[1:4])
})
rownames(counts) <- names(txt)[1:4]
counts
hr_set_tokenizer(prev_tok)
```

Both count below the heuristic on every row, and `"chars"` counts 11
Japanese characters as 3 tokens. A low count is the direction that overruns a
window, so keep the heuristic unless you have a counter that matches your
model.

### Plugging in a real tokenizer

`hr_set_tokenizer("tiktoken")` switches to OpenAI's tokenizer, through the
reticulate package and Python's `tiktoken`:

```{r eval = FALSE}
hr_set_tokenizer("tiktoken")
hr_count_tokens("The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.", model = "gpt-4o")
```

Given a `model` that `tiktoken` knows, it counts in that model's encoding.
Without one, which is how harnessr's own budgets call it, it counts in both
encodings current OpenAI models use (`cl100k_base` and `o200k_base`) and keeps
the larger. For a model from another provider the count is an estimate with
none of the heuristic's padding. Without reticulate or `tiktoken`,
`hr_set_tokenizer("tiktoken")` stops with an error and the tokenizer stays as
it was: a silent fallback would change every budget without a word.

For any other model, register a counter of your own: a function that takes a
character vector and returns one count per element. A provider's tokenizer
wrapped in R goes here. This one stands in for it with a rule of thumb of 3
characters per token:

```{r}
hr_set_tokenizer("three_chars", function(x) ceiling(nchar(x) / 3))
hr_tokenizer()
hr_count_tokens(txt)
```

`hr_set_tokenizer()` registers the function under the name and makes it the
active counter; from then on, `hr_set_tokenizer("three_chars")` switches back to
it by name. The counter gets the text alone, not the model. harnessr sets a
negative or `NA` count to 0, and stops if the function returns the wrong number
of counts. A counter you register is copied to the workers of a parallel run,
with the models you registered.

### Where a count shows up

A result's `usage` says where its token counts came from. A backend that
returns plain text reports none, so harnessr counted the prompt and the reply
itself:

```{r}
res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "gpt-4o-mini")
str(res$usage)
```

`provenance` is `"reported"` when the provider gave the figures,
`"counted"` when harnessr counted them with `tiktoken`, and `"estimated"` with
any other counter, the one in use here. A count made with a crude counter can
undercount a request's cost, so an estimated usage is worth checking against
the provider's bill on a real run.

```{r}
hr_set_tokenizer(prev_tok)
```

## Choosing the settings

Four options decide how the registry and the counter behave. Each walkthrough
says what the option controls, the signs that point to changing it, where its
default came from, and how to test a change.

### Unknown models: `unknown_model_action` {#set-unknown-model}

**What it controls.** What a lookup does when the registry does not hold the
id: `"warn"` (the default) guesses from a family pattern or the default
profile and warns with class `gr_unknown_model`; `"error"` stops with an error
of that class, so no request goes out with guessed limits.

**Signs it needs changing.** A `gr_unknown_model` warning in a run you meant to
send to a known model is a typo or a new model. On a scheduled or unattended
run, set `"error"`, since nobody reads the warning before the run spends.

**Where the default came from.** `"warn"` lets a first run with a new model
work. `gr_settings_table("options")` declares no evidence for it.

**How to test it.** Look up every id a script uses under `"error"` before the
run:

```{r}
prev <- hr_options(unknown_model_action = "error")
ids <- c("gpt-4o", "chatgpt-4o-latest", "gpt-5.6-tera")
vapply(ids, function(id) {
  tryCatch(hr_model_info(id)$source, gr_unknown_model = function(e) "unknown")
}, "")
hr_options(prev)
```

### Models with no price: `allow_unpriced` {#set-unpriced}

**What it controls.** Whether a request to a chat model with no price is sent
while `max_cost_usd` is set. `TRUE`, the default, sends it, records its cost as
`NA` and warns once per model with class `hr_unpriced_model`. `FALSE` refuses
it with a condition of that class.

**Signs it needs changing.** An `hr_unpriced_model` warning, or `NA` in the
`usd` column of `hr_trace_cost()`, on a run whose cost has to stay under a
limit. Set the model's prices; set `allow_unpriced = FALSE` when a run must
never spend outside the limit.

**Where the default came from.** harnessr ships no prices, so `FALSE` would
refuse every request to a built-in model until you set its prices.
`gr_settings_table("options")` lists it as untested.

**How to test it.** Check which models a run names have a price before you
send anything:

```{r}
run_models <- c("gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "unpriced-model")
do.call(rbind, lapply(run_models, hr_estimate_cost, input_tokens = 0, detail = TRUE))
```

### How old a price may be: `price_max_age_days` {#set-price-age}

**What it controls.** The age in days, counted from the first day of a price's
`as_of` month, past which a cost computed from the price warns with class
`hr_stale_price`. `NULL` turns the warning off. The warning changes no figure
and stops nothing.

**Signs it needs changing.** A stale warning on prices you checked recently
means the `as_of` in your file is behind; update it rather than the option.
Raise the limit for a provider whose prices you know have not moved, such as a
contract price.

**Where the default came from.** 120 days, about four months, so prices set
once are checked again a few times a year. `gr_settings_table("options")` lists
it as untested.

**How to test it.** `hr_models()` shows the month of every price, and the age
in days follows from it:

```{r}
m <- hr_models()
p <- m[!is.na(m$input_usd_per_1m), c("id", "as_of")]
p$age_days <- as.numeric(Sys.Date() - as.Date(paste0(p$as_of, "-01")))
p
```

### The token counter: `tokenizer` {#set-tokenizer}

**What it controls.** Which counter `hr_count_tokens()` uses, and so every
budget, every cut to a number of tokens and every usage figure the provider
did not report. Set it with `hr_set_tokenizer()`, which checks the name and,
for `"tiktoken"`, that Python's package is there.

**Signs it needs changing.** A provider error that a prompt was too long means
the counter came in under. Usage marked `"estimated"` that differs much from
the provider's bill is the other sign. With OpenAI models and Python at hand,
`"tiktoken"` gives exact counts.

**Where the default came from.** The heuristic needs nothing installed and is
built to come out high; its calibration is described above.
`gr_settings_table("options")` declares no evidence for it.

**How to test it.** Count a sample of your own text with each counter you
consider, and compare the counts with the prompt tokens your provider reports
for the same text:

```{r}
sample_text <- c("Net revenue rose 12% to $45.2 million in fiscal 2024.",
                 "| segment | 2023 | 2024 |\n| retail | 38.1 | 45.2 |")
sapply(c("heuristic", "words", "chars"), function(t) {
  hr_set_tokenizer(t)
  hr_count_tokens(sample_text)
})
hr_set_tokenizer(prev_tok)
```

## Where the document layer builds on this

The segmenters size chunks with `hr_count_tokens()`, the readers fit each
prompt to the model's window from `hr_model_info()`, and every cost the
document layer reports comes from these prices. `vignette("runs")` sets prices
for a whole document run and shows the costs it reports.

```{r include = FALSE}
hr_options(old)
```
